title: The Problem of Induction in Philosophy
text:
The problem of induction, famously articulated by David Hume, questions the logical basis for inferring future instances from past observations. At its core, it highlights that while observed regularities suggest predictable patterns—such as the sun rising each morning—there is no deductive guarantee that this pattern will continue indefinitely.

Philosophically, this implies that empirical knowledge does not provide absolute certainty regarding causality or universal laws. The belief in causation remains a powerful assumption of human reasoning and scientific methodology, despite its lack of strict logical proof.

Alternative approaches to the problem have included recognizing it as a methodological necessity rather than an epistemological failing. Instead of seeking infallible justification for prediction, focus shifts toward evaluating the reliability and scope of observational data within defined systems.
